strengths: Introduces a genuinely unified, modular VRP environment that can represent 48 variants through simple attribute on/off composition, a 3x increase in variant coverage over prior multi-task VRP work (MTPOMO, MVMoE), which is a valuable engineering and benchmarking contribution to the community.

The set of proposed components (modern Transformer encoder with RMSNorm/SwiGLU/pre-norm/FlashAttention, Global Attribute Embeddings, Mixed Batch Training, multi-task reward normalization, Efficient Adapter Layers) is well-motivated and each is separately ablated, showing consistent, if individually modest, additive gains (Figure 5, Appendices D.3-D.6).

Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) is a simple, well-justified idea (zero-padding new attribute dimensions rather than reinitializing adapter layers) that empirically preserves zero-shot performance at 'step 0' and clearly outperforms the AL baseline from Lin et al. (2024), with the advantage growing as the finetuning task becomes harder (MB -> MD -> MB&MD), which is a convincing and practically useful result.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 48 in-distribution variants at two sizes, out-of-distribution attribute-value generalization (capacity, time windows, duration limits), large-scale CVRPLIB real-world instances, and t-SNE interpretability analysis of the learned latent space, giving a fairly thorough picture of the model's behavior beyond simple average-gap tables.

Good reproducibility: detailed architecture equations, hyperparameters (Table 4), licensing table, and environment logic (masking rules) are all documented in the appendix, and code is stated to be publicly released.
weaknesses: The headline claim of '>10% gap reduction' is a relative improvement over already-small absolute gaps (e.g., MTPOMO 1.99% vs RF-TE 1.51% on CVRP n=100); the practical significance of these differences, especially relative to the much larger gap to HGS-PyVRP/OR-Tools, is not strongly established, and no variance/seed-level statistics are reported to assess robustness of the differences.

The contribution is largely a combination of known techniques adapted to the VRP setting (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, pre-norm, FlashAttention from LLM literature; attribute composition from Liu et al. 2024a/Zhou et al. 2024) rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea, making the novelty primarily architectural/engineering rather than conceptual.

The paper's own conclusion acknowledges that ROUTEFINDER trades off in-distribution solution quality compared to single-variant specialist models, and Table 13 confirms single-variant POMO models can be competitive on tasks matching their training distribution (e.g., POMO_VRPB on backhaul variants), leaving the practical trade-off between the foundation-model approach and specialized models under-quantified.

The paper's backhaul definition intentionally deviates from prevailing ML-literature convention (Liu et al. 2024a; Zhou et al. 2024), which, while justified by OR literature, complicates direct numerical comparison with prior published NCO backhaul results and could confuse readers/reproducers who are unaware of the change.

Evaluation relies solely on greedy decoding with multistart + 8x augmentation; no comparison to more powerful inference-time strategies (beam search, active search, sampling) that some baselines and follow-up works use, potentially limiting the strength of the 'outperforms SOTA' claim under different inference budgets.

Non-standard time-window and demand generation procedures (rather than, e.g., the widely used Solomon benchmark protocol) may reduce comparability of absolute numbers with the broader VRP-TW literature, an issue the authors partially acknowledge but do not fully address with a matching-protocol comparison in the main results.

strengths: The unified attribute-composition VRP environment covering 48 variants is a useful engineering contribution and is described with substantial implementation detail (Appendix A), which aids reproducibility.

The EAL zero-padding idea for finetuning to unseen attributes is a sensible, simple, and well-motivated design choice, and the 'step 0' comparison against AL convincingly shows it avoids the performance collapse of randomly-initialized adapters.
Extensive ablations (encoder components, reward normalization variants, MBT stabilization, t-SNE analyses) are provided, giving some insight into which pieces matter.
The empirical scope (48 variants, OOD attribute studies, CVRPLIB) is broader than prior multi-task VRP papers.
weaknesses: The core architectural contribution is largely a repackaging of well-known, off-the-shelf tricks (RMSNorm, pre-norm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) applied to the existing POMO/AM encoder; there is little conceptual novelty here beyond engineering integration, and the ablation (Fig. 5/6) shows these changes yield only marginal gains (~0.1-0.3% gap) over MTPOMO/MVMoE baselines that were not given the same modernization for fair isolation of the encoder's effect.

The headline claim of '>10% gap reduction across all variants' (abstract, intro) is not well supported by Table 1: the actual relative improvements of RF-TE over MTPOMO/MVMoE are frequently under 5% relative reduction in gap (e.g., CVRP n=100: 1.505% vs 1.694%/1.988%), and no statistical evidence is given to support the claimed magnitude uniformly across all 48 variants.

No variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere (Tables 1, 2, 9-13), despite RL training being known to be high-variance; this makes many fine-grained comparisons (e.g., RF-MoE vs RF-TE swapping best/second-best across rows) unreliable and hard to assess for significance.

Mixed Batch Training and Multi-Task Reward Normalization are incremental adaptations of standard multi-task learning and reward-scaling ideas well established in the RL literature, rebranded with new names; the novelty claimed for these components appears overstated relative to prior multi-task RL/curriculum work.

The comparison baselines (MTPOMO, MVMoE) are handicapped: the paper changes the training protocol (all-variant sampling vs. the original single-attribute sampling used by these baselines) simultaneously with introducing MBT, encoder changes, and reward normalization, making it hard to isolate whether gains stem from the proposed techniques or simply from more/different training data exposure; the ablation study does not fully disentangle this confound.

In the EAL finetuning experiments, the compared 'AL' baseline is reimplemented from Lin et al. rather than validated against its original best configuration, and no hyperparameter tuning details or sensitivity analysis for AL are given, raising fairness-of-comparison concerns.

Absolute solution quality still lags traditional solvers (PyVRP/HGS) by several percentage points across nearly all variants and instance sizes, and the paper's own conclusion admits reduced in-distribution quality versus single-task models, yet this practical limitation is understated in the abstract/introduction's 'foundation model' framing.

The Impact Statement is a boilerplate one-liner that does not engage with dual-use, deployment, or compute/environmental considerations despite the paper's own foundation-model framing and substantial reported GPU-hour training costs.

strengths: Very comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 48 VRP variants (3x prior multi-task learning work), with consistent improvements over MTPOMO and MVMoE baselines across nearly all settings and problem sizes (n=50, n=100).

The unified attribute-composition VRP environment is a clean, extensible abstraction that cleanly unifies node and global attributes (capacity, backhauls, time windows, multi-depot, open routes, duration limits, mixed backhauls) into a single MDOVRPMBLTW environment, with clear documentation of the action-masking logic in the appendix.

Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) are a simple but effective idea: zero-padding new attribute dimensions preserves the pretrained model's zero-shot behavior exactly at fine-tuning initialization ('step 0'), unlike the AL baseline (Lin et al. 2024) which severely degrades performance before any fine-tuning steps. This is empirically well demonstrated in Table 2 and further validated on multi-depot and combined MB+MD unseen-attribute settings in the appendix.

Thorough ablation studies (architecture components, reward normalization variants, mixed batch training) isolate the contribution of each proposed technique, and t-SNE visualizations provide reasonable interpretability evidence that Global Attribute Embeddings produce more separable latent clusters than baselines.

Strong reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters (Table 4), licenses for all used assets, extensive appendix documentation of data generation and environment logic, and publicly released code.

Additional generalization experiments (out-of-distribution attribute values, large-scale CVRPLIB instances) strengthen the claim that the foundation-model approach generalizes better than single-variant models trained under the same budget, which is a meaningful practical finding.
weaknesses: The abstract's claim of '>10% reduction in optimality gaps' is a relative reduction in gap percentage, not absolute; absolute improvements over MTPOMO/MVMoE in Table 1 are often modest (fractions of a percentage point in objective gap), which could be over-stated by the framing.

Several architectural contributions (RMSNorm, pre-norm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are directly imported from recent LLM architecture literature rather than being novel to the VRP/CO setting; the paper is transparent about this but it somewhat limits the originality claim of the 'modern transformer encoder' contribution.

The reward normalization ablation (Figure 8, Appendix D.4) shows a very small effect size (differences in the fourth decimal of average gap), raising questions about whether this specific contribution is empirically load-bearing versus other components (MBT, transformer encoder, global embeddings) which show clearer gains in Figure 5.

ROUTEFINDER still trails substantially behind the traditional OR solver (HGS-PyVRP) in solution quality across all variants (1-5% optimality gap even in-distribution), which is acknowledged but somewhat tempers the 'foundation model' framing's practical readiness.

No direct empirical comparison to other recent VRP foundation/multi-task approaches mentioned in related work (e.g., GOAL, UNCO, Wang & Yu's bandit method), limiting the completeness of the SOTA comparison beyond MTPOMO/MVMoE.

The paper's redefinition of 'backhaul' relative to prior ML papers (Liu et al. 2024a; Zhou et al. 2024) is explained but creates a subtle incompatibility that could confuse readers comparing numbers across papers, even though the authors justify it via OR literature convention.
